projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William Huebner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: February 22, 2004. I'm interviewing William Huebner from Avon. Interviewer is Eileen Hurst __ from Central Connecticut State University. Bill, will you tell me your full name, your birth date, and your current address.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: William J. Huebner. 111 __ Road, Avon.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And your birth date?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: July 27, 1925 which was a very good year.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What war were you in and what branch of the service?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: World War II, U.S. Army and Korea, U.S. Army.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And what was your rank?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Corporal in World War II and Staff Sergeant in Korea.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Going back to when you first joined the army, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I was drafted in 1943.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember the month?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: March.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Watertown Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: When you were drafted in the army, did you have thoughts of joining another branch of the service or were you Okay with the Army?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I originally signed up for the U.S. Airforce when I was 17. At that time they were taking high school seniors at age 17 and then bringing them into the airforce for cadet training when they turned 18 and that's how I got in it. Eileen Hurst:: So did you join when you were 17 years old at the time?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I was 17 and I went into the U.S. Air Corps. There wasn't any United States Air Corps. Army Air Corps, and I was sent to Miami beach for basic training and then Gulfport, Mississippi for flight training and I washed off because my eyes went back, from 20/20 to 20/30. And they wanted to send me to gunnery school, but I was too tall. I was 6'3. Then they said they were going to make me an aircraft mechanic, and I didn't care for that and at that time you could volunteer for the infantry or the paratroopers, and I volunteered for the infantry. The next day I was put on a train to San Francisco and heading for New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Wow. When you first joined the Army Air Corps and went to Miami, did you do basic training in Miami?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And how long was that?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: About a month, two months.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What was basic training like in Miami?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, marching, rifle sidearm firing, that's about it.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And then from Miami you went...

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Gulfport, Mississippi.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Gulfport?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Gulfport, Mississippi.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And what kind of training did they do there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I think the old piper aircraft and Stearman 17 biplanes and that only lasted about two months until they caught up with my eyes, and I got taken out of flight training.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you actually do anything in the aircraft before then?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Before they caught your eyes.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you have bad vision before you went in?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. It seems overnight that it went from 20/20 to 20/30 and I just couldn't read the 20/20 line on the chart and that's how they caught it. I just woke up one morning and I couldn't see the leaves on the tree.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Was that a disappointment for you?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, yes. As a matter of fact, I went to the nearest store and bought ten cans of carrot juice. They said carrot juice would improve your eyesight. I drank the damn stuff and it tasted lousy, but it didn't help the eyesight.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So then you joined the infantry?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Camp Stoneman, California.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Camp Stoneman?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, no. Wait a minute. Camp Kearns in Utah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Was that more training there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: More training and we actually got mountain training and cold weather training and we thought we were getting ready to go to Italy or some other place where there's mountains and snow, but, and we were issued heavy clothing. Then all of a sudden overnight we had to get on trucks or trains in Frisco and we were shipped out to the South Pacific.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How much notice did you have? Overnight?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. Overnight.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you know at the time where you were going?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So then they put you on ships in San Francisco?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. The ship was the motor ship __ __. It was a Dutch cargo vessel that carried about two hundred men. Now, we were all replacements infantry replacements, rifle men. Oh, about seven days out we were in a convoy at night, we were zigzagging and we were hit by another American ship broadside and we had to abandon ship. The ship didn't sink, but they put in the water on rafts and when dawn came up we could see the ship that hit us because their bow was caved in and our ship had a big hole in the middle. So we got back on that ship that was leaking badly and it was towed actually to Espiritu Santo in the New Hebrides Islands. Espiritu Santo was a beautiful island. French island and they made the movie South Pacific on it. It was a most wonderful island and we stayed there until another ship came and we boarded that and we ended up in the invasion of New Guinea, British New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember how long it took to cross to New Guinea from when you left San Francisco?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, because we had to go on to the island, I think we lost about two months.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So you worked two months at getting the boat fixed?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Holy cow. That must have been pretty scary when you're just a young guy and you're just on the boat and you hear it crash.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: When you're young, nothing scares you.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors from basic training?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: They were all sergeants and they were all southern boys. And I remember the first time we lined up for role call, there was this big old southern sergeant came in and said, "Now, I want y'all to hep me," and we figured "hep" is hep hep hep, you know. But he meant, "I want you all to help me." So we had to learn the southern language being Yankees from Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Any memorable experiences from basic training either at Miami, Mississippi, or Utah?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Miami was wonderful. We were living in a big luxury hotel and ate in a dining room. Mississippi, I think I remember about Mississippi is in the barracks, they burned soft coal. That's all you could smell all day long was this soft coal burning. And, of course, out in Utah it was cold. We were up in the mountains. And I must say the one thing, I was all on Thanksgiving Day and we were invited to Thanksgiving dinner and there was three of us by a Mormon family and they put on a tremendous feed for us that I'll never forget it. I'm not a Mormon, but I'll never forget the hospitality of the Mormon people.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Where did you exactly land in New Guinea? Do you remember the landing?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Finch Haven. Finch Haven was a coconut plantation in British New Guinea and was owned by for hundred of years by Palmolive-Peet. And they used to make Palmolive soap and they used the coconut oil to make the soap. The coconut plantation was about, oh, maybe a hundred square miles up and down the coast, but beyond that was the jungle and that's where the Japanese were. We started going after the Japs, but we started losing too money men and MacArthur made a decision. He said contain them, don't go after them. Just keep them in there and let them get hungry and starve which we did until we were taken over by another unit where we could contain them in the jungles.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember what the date was when you arrived in New Guinea? Was it still in 1943?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: In '43, late '43; yes

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And what was your specific job?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I was a rifleman.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What are the duties of a rifleman? What would your day be like?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Shoot a rifle at the enemy. We were given a Garand rifle. We were trained in it and we were also trained in the Johnson submachine gun and the M1A1 Carbine, but basically, I was a rifleman.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What was barracks life like?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: In New Guinea.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: There wasn't any.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you have a camp?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: On the ground.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you have a camp or were you constantly on the move and in a different place?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: We were constantly on the move.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: There was no base camp where you were at for any length of time?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. We even had kitchens that followed us, portable kitchens. If you want to call them kitchens. It was just a place to heat up the sea rations.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How many casualties were there in your unit?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, when I replaced them, they had quite a few casualties because they went after the Japanese, and the Japanese can hide in the jungle and one man can pick off three or four men and that's why it was useless to go after them in the jungle because we couldn't win. And MacArthur says, leave them alone, and contain them, let them get hungry. I ended up in a corporal end. So I had a squad and I only lost one man because I made sure that they didn't go after the Japanese.Eileen Hurst:: How much men in a squad?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: At that time, the old squad was about 12 men.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Were you ever a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Can you remember any memorable experiences in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, aside from being harassed by Japanese, __, and rifle fire, we got hit in the swamps of New Guinea with leeches. We'd have to wade through the swamps and maybe 12 hours after that where we got through with our mission, our boots were all warm. When we took them off, the blood came out of them. Well, these leeches drop off the trees into the water and went into our boots and of course little tiny things, but when they got through sucking all your blood, they blow up as big as a walnut. And we got them in our boots and we'd swash them when they were full and we were walking around in our own blood. And that's one way I got what they call dengue fever, from leeches. And they used to drop off the trees down your back. And they're very hard to take off. You can't scrape them off with a knife because it leaves their fangs in your skin and then the infections go in through the fangs. You got to burn them off with a cigarette butt. You put a cigarette butt at the end near their head and they with draw their fangs. Either that or you got to put alcohol, but we didn't have any alcohol. Whatever alcohol that was available, we drank.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Well, so you had dengue fever when you were over there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes. I also had malaria.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did that give you...did you stay on duty or did you spend did you spend time in a hospital over there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. Quite a few of us had malaria and what they did we had to take Atabrine tablets and that held down the malaria so you could function. Some people had to go to a hospital. And these hospitals were just big long tents. And those who didn't take Atabrine, they got the sweats and the shakes, the sweats and the chills from malaria, but they could face a Court Marshal if they didn't take their Atabrine tablets. And one thing about Atabrine, you knew if you were taking them or not taking them because they turned you yellow. Underneath here (Indicating the neck) all yellow, under your armpits, all yellow because Atabrine was yellow anyway.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How do you spell it?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: A-t-a-b-r-i-n-e. It's a replacement for a synthetic replacement for quinine. The Americans lost all their sources of quinine when the Japanese took over Borneo, Sumatra, and the other areas. So they came up with this synthetic quinine called Atabrine and it worked.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How sick were you from the dengue fever?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, now, I think I only lost...pulled out of the line for maybe one or two days the maximum.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Were you awarded any metals or citations?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, I got the... Where? In New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, I qualified for the Asiatic-Pacific metal with one battle star at that time. We moved from British New Guinea up to Dutch New Guinea. It was Hollandia and it was an old mining town in New Guinea. New Guinea is the second largest island in the world. Greenland being the largest island. So New Guinea was divided between the British and the Dutch. And Hollandia was a mining community for the Dutch, also gold mining. And we landed short of Hollandia and went up and took the main town, but primarily the airstrips. The Japanese had about ten airstrips in and around Hollandia and our job was to destroy and get rid of them and destroy whatever we could destroy. In case we had to leave they couldn't have their gasoline stores depos, ammunition depos, food depos. So it was a pretty tough battle for New Guinea for a while. My unit wasn't the only one involved in it. The 11th Airborne Division had one of the first paratroop jumps on New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What was your unit?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: The 595th Signal Aircraft Warning Battalion and that was a rather unique organization. It was only a battalion. My job was to provide security for these radar technicians. This is portable radar and they would go in and onto small islands and sometimes without any Japanese on them and set up this portable radar to cover areas that the big radar cannot cover. Because the Japanese used to go on the deck between the islands and the big radar couldn't pick them up and then all of a sudden you had fighters on top of you. So with this portable radar the signal aircraft warning battalion would pick them up. Pick them up about 20 miles away and radio back that they're coming in through these blind spots and it worked. The anti-aircraft people had at least 10-20 minutes to get ready for the arrival of these aircrafts. Usually they were single-engine fighters that are out trying to destroy our ammunition dumps, our food dumps, gasoline dumps, and ships. And my job, of course, was provide security. We did land on other islands. You know, there's thousands of islands in the South Pacific. We landed on some islands and nobody was there and we set up. Other times it was a Japanese weather station and we landed and then we had to go and eliminate those men operating that weather station. Do it quietly so they couldn't radio that their station was being intercepted. Other times we ran into a battalion of Japanese and once we got on there, we had to pull back and we did it in rubber boats and we usually it at night. But once they got set up, I established a perimeter around the men operating these radar units, the small radar units, and my job was not to shoot but to protect them and try to keep it as quiet as possible. If we were discovered, we had to fight, but...

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Were you ever discovered?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. We were discovered and we had...Well, we had to destroy the equipment and race back to the place we landed and we had little rubber boats and get on there and go back out to sea, but we had a radio and there were boats out there to pick us up.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: When you'd go on these mission to these __, how big a group of men would you take? Just a 12 man squad or...

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: A 12 man squad was only four rifleman. The rest were radar technicians.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So there were only four of you that were protecting them?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. That's all they needed because, again I say, it wasn't our job to engage in combat. It was to avoid it. To get there quietly and let no one know you were there.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you get any other medals during World War II?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. Philippine Liberation. We got one from... Oh, from British New Guinea Medal and from the Dutch government from Holland for the liberation of their part of New Guinea, and I think that was about it.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Where did you go from Dutch New Guinea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: The Biak Island.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Biak?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Biak, B-i-a-k. That was a big island between the top of New Guinea and the bottom of Borneo, and we set up our units facing Borneo because the Japanese had airfields on Borneo, and we had to get an advance warning to the troops that were hitting the bottom of Biak Island. And it was about a two months operation. We were successful. We got a lot of the incoming aircraft and alerted the troops that the aircraft were coming after them and they could take preventive measures.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: It was be 1944 by now.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And where did you go after Biak Island?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Owi Island, O-w-i. It's a very small island oh, about 20 miles off Biak Island, and we were going to set up a unit... a portable radar unit to cover a certain dead spot on the approach to Biak and we landed on Owi. Owi was only two miles long and one mile wide. It was supposed to be deserted and we went in there what they call "standing up." Well, there was about 30 Japanese on the island. Most of them were mechanics because there was one air strip on Owi Island. And most of the Japanese were mechanics, aircraft mechanics, and there were a few that were trained in the use of rifle machine guns. And all of a sudden we got all this machine gun fire and we say, where the hell are these people coming from? And the guy say, well they're only supposed to be mechanics. And I said, well, mechanics aren't supposed to shoot like that, but we found out they did. So we had to call in support. And we actually called in Air Support to bomb these positions. And we finally got rid of them. It was a big surprise to us.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Where did you go from Owi Island?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Owi Island we staged for the invasion of the Philippines. The first was the "lady island." We weren't involved in that. Ours was Luzon Island, the major island in the Philippines. And we landed in the Gulf of Lingayen which was oh, about 10-200 miles above Manila. And we went in a place called Dagopin (phonetic), and we staged there and went out to set up our units in a northern part of the Luzon Island because the Japanese had aircraft coming from Formosa to bomb the American ships that were starting to land troops. A lot of the Formosin aircraft were coming on the deck. The big radar couldn't pick them up. So we... our unit could pick them up even when they were skimming the water. Now, I couldn't, but the technicians could and it was very very active at that time. And we went all the way up the northern Luzon setting up these units because a lot of small islands in between and surprising the Japanese might have an air strip maybe 5,000 feet long and they would have two or three fighters on it. They were undocumented. We didn't know they were there until they took off, well camouflaged too. But the trouble is they were running out of gasoline, but when they had enough gas, they came after us. So we ended up in the northern part of Luzon Island. And then we went down south, again I don't know, I think we were supposed to invade Formosa which was a major Japanese base which is now Taiwan. We were going down to Manila which was just about taken by American forces except for the "Walled city of Manila." A little Spanish historic area and the Japanese wouldn't surrender and the Americans had to clobber it with artillery and everything else to get them out. They couldn't come out. They died in there, but I saw what the Japanese did to the Filipino people in Manila. They kill them, they slaughtered them, they were mad at them and they just went on a rampage and dead civilians are laying in the street all over while the war was going on and they weren't killed by the Americans. They were killed by the Japanese because the Filipinos were helping the Americans, throughout the war they were. The Filipino guerillas. But it was a hell of a slaughter.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: After Manila, where did you go?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Home sweet home.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember the date or what month and year?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, I was released from active duty on December 5th, 1945. Took us two months on the ship again.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: To get home?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. Well, we landed at San Francisco and then got on a train to cross the United States and that was a long trip too and we ended at Fort Devens, Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: While you were overseas during the war, how did you stay in touch with family?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: V mail.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: V mail?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Can you explain what that was.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: V mail, you write a letter and the army takes a photograph of it. Might put it on microfilm and ship it over and then they reproduce it in a letter. They put it on a little microfilm, the letter. So they could handle a lot of V mail.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: That must have taken quite a while for you to correspond to send one home and did the letters come back the same way?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. The letters came back as regular mail.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What was the food like while you were overseas?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Rotten. We were on the move all the time so when we weren't on the move because we were only a battalion, we'd be assigned to eat with some regiment and which was at rest. So they had these portable kitchens. So you got hot corn beef, hash, powdered milk, powdered eggs, powdered lemon juice, lemonade. Sometimes we'd get what they called "bully beef", Australian beef. It was tough. Of course, if you boiled the hell out of it, it would soften up, but it was meat. So that was it. Accept for when we were on an operation, we didn't have anything. We had k rations. Sea rations or k rations. They call field rations. It was just emergency rations to keep you alive.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Could you feel any pressure or stress while you were overseas doing your job?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you do anything special for good luck?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Do what?

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Good luck. You know, some guys have rabbit foots.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you get to see any parts of the countries while you were overseas? Did you get to go anywhere else and visit anything?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Visit anything? I went where I was told to go. I didn't visit any place.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Every place that you went, you guys were walking to get there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: All right. For the record, Bill does have photographs that will be included. Do you remember any of your fellow soldiers or officers?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: From World War II?

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, yeah. There was a battalion Sergeant Major his name was Saunders and he was from Texas. He was a good man. A good master sergeant. I worked under a staff sergeant...I forget his name now. They were all older. Don't forget, I was young and they were all older. That's about it. We were a very small unit.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Your squad was only 12. How big would a battalion be? How many in a battalion.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, a battalions got 1500 men, a 1,000 to 1,500.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended from World War II?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. December 5th, 1945.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What did it feel like getting out of the service?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I didn't get of the service. I signed up in the Reserves.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Why did you do that?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, they said to keep your rank and stay in long enough, you get a pension.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What was your rank at that time?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Corporal.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So when you were in the Reserves you could still go home and do weekends...

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I went...I got released from active duty and accepted in the Reserves, Army Reserves and I went home and I went to college.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Where did you go to college?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Suffolk University in Boston Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What university?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Suffolk University. A great university. The front door of the university was the back door of the State Capitol. The back door of the university was the back door of the Old Howard Burlesque at Scollay Square. So we were in a class in the summer the windows were open, we would hear the chorus girls doing their bumps and grinds rehearsals.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And what degree did you get from the university?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I didn't get any. I took a job as running a weekly newspaper in Harwich, Massachusetts, a weekly newspaper. Why did I do this? I met a guy, Senator Harry Harborgh (phonetic), State Senator and I was in the college of journalism for the Suffolk University. He stopped by one time. He said, young man, I got, I own a newspaper down at Cape Cod, how'd you like to run it for me? I said, sure. It was my summer vacation. I'll do it. I said, how much? He said I can't pay you much, but I'll give you room and board which was good. I later found out he owned a restaurant down there called the Red Sail Restaurant. So that's where we ate. He owned the barn where the parsonage, congregational parsonage, stored their equipment, but there was a room above the barn and he let us sleep up there on cots but, again, we were young.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So you didn't go back to school in the fall?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, yeah I went back to school and he says I'm going to keep the paper going all year long. Harwich, Cape Cod is a very small town.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What was the name of the paper?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Harwich Independent. So he says, why don't you come down here for the winter and run it and see what youcan do. I was thinking maybe I could buy the place. So I worked there in the winter. The one thing about that newspaper we had a circulation of 500 in the winter, 5,000 in the summer because all the summer residents would pick it up at the stores. They had subscriptions and stuff and the advertising came from the A and P and the First National and the auto dealerships and the play houses. One of my most memorable occasions on the Cape was we used to get passes to the summer play housesand plus they used to have a cocktail hour, a little food, and we always took advantage of it. But I interviewed Edward Everett Horton. The older people will know who he was. Very nice guy, a veteran actor. And he invited me back stage and showed me how the act did make-up, how they learned their lines, and everything else. A very nice man. I never forgot it. That was quite an experience to meet a person like him.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you... when you went to Suffolk University, was that supported by the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So how did you end up staying on the newspaper? You never went back to school after that?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: You stayed in Cape Cod?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. I enjoyed it. I jacked up the circulation, the revenue, and everything down there. I actually took two of my friends from the university to work with me and they were getting dissatisfied. So I had a staff of two men and they sold advertising and did stories and hustled circulation. And I don't mean over the counter circulation. I mean a year round circulation and we did pretty well on it. One guy left for... eventually ended up in Indiana working and the other one was... became an actor. But we had a grand time down there the three of us. The names were Richard Powers and Dick Powers. I played the accordion and he played the guitar and we used to go to amateurs hours down at the Cape during the summer.You win prizes: $5, $10, everything else. Depends on how much the audience would applaud, but the third member was Eddy Pearl. He was a handsome kid. Black Irish, black Irish eyes, and he had a voice that would melt your heart. A real Irish tenor. We used to go in and we'd win all the time. We'd get $5, $10, $15 at these amateur nights because of his singing and I was a lousy accordion player, but I could play Wild Irish Rose, I'll Take You Home, Kathleen. But he used to make it. He was a hell of a singer and I guess me eventually became some type of a professional singer after a while.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you stay in touch with any soldiers that you knew from World War II after the war?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: All right. Now, I understand you were also in Korea. So how'd you go from running a newspaper to going to Korea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I got a letter, a telegram, from the government that said you got to report to the army base for a routine physical.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember the year?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: What? The year?

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: It was 1950. Right after the Korea War started. So I reported to the boss on the army base, got my physical, and they said all right you're being recalled. I say, what do you mean? They said, well you're going to Korea because what they were taking were infantry, armored, and artillery because that's what they needed mostly in Korea. So I was given 30 days to rap up my affairs et cetera et cetera and they put me on a train to Fort Campbell, Kentucky. And we were trained this time I was about 26 years old. I was getting fat, smoking too much, drinking too much, and out of shape. And we started getting trained by these 18 and 19 year old paratroopers in Fort Campbell, Kentucky and they just about killed us. Double timing here, double timing there, doing push-ups and everything else. Well they got us into shape, but just about killed us. As a matter of fact, it got so bad I quit smoking.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Wow. So did you have to go through the whole same basic training all over?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. But it was very quick. It was 30 days.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: 30 days for basic training?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: That's all. Well, we were all veterans anyway. We all had it before, but we had to get in the new... Well, the recoilless rifle which I didn't operate because I was still a basic rifleman.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So what did you use?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Rifle. M1 Garand.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Was that the same one that you used in World War II?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: That's right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So that was familiar to you.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: After your 30 day basic training, where did you go?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Right to San Francisco in the boat. That was the quickest operation we had.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Wow. And from San Francisco you went over to Korea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. Puson.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember landing what it was like?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. It was cold and raining and we were put into a replacements camp on the side of a hill outside of Puson. And we were given new clothes, new fatigues, and a new pair of boots because our boots were not combat boots. And we were given, sort of a winter jacket, and a bandoleer of ammunition, and cartridge belt, and canteen, and all the other things. So they got us jeered up pretty well for combat.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And did you see combat over there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. Right...I think a week later I was assigned to the Third Infantry Division. The Third Infantry Division was an old line division dating back to World War I. It's also called the __ __ and the... but it all had young kids, young draftees in it that never experienced combat. And we were veterans of World War II and went through a war. And we were put in charge of these kids and they didn't know enough to duck. A lot of them got their heads blown off because they weren't trained. They were quickly trained, but then sent over there as canon fouter and we were sent over there to shape them up. The problem we had, I was a corporal at that time, they made me a platoon leader. Now, why would they make a corporal a platoon leader? Number one, I had experience of combat in World War II and there was no second lieutenants. Normally, there would be platoon leaders. So for this reason the graduating West Point Class of 1949/1950 were wiped out in Korea. They were all young 2nd lieutenants. They trained platoon leaders. Why? And I saw it happen, they were all gun hoe. They'd stand up and say, follow me. As soon as they did that, they got mowed down. Now, the more experienced people like myself and others say, the hell with that. Duck and shoot, then duck again, and then shoot again. Never mind standing up and being a hero because you're going to get killed. So wait until you got a good target in site. So we brought a leveling influence to the youngsters in the platoon. As soon as they realized that we were, as squad leaders and platoon leaders, that we were concerned about their welfare, we didn't want to lose them because they leave a hole in the platoon. And our job was to hold at that time and we didn't want to lose our men through heroics. So that was our job to straighten it up.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you lose any of your men in your unit?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: When I was a staff sergeant, I did.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: When you were a platoon leader, when you went over, did you go over with any guys, like, from your Reserves? Was it all guys you knew from World War II?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: ...or was it all new guys?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: All new guys. We were all in the Unorganized Inactive Reserves. In other words, we were a pool of canon fouter. So that's what we were. We weren't in any Reserve Units or... we were all individuals.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What were living conditions like in Korea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Terrible.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: As bad as World War II?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, we didn't have the bugs and everything else in Korea, but we were either retreating or advancing. So you never set up any permanent facilities.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So once again you're sleeping outside on the ground?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. And one of the troubles there in the winter of 1950, we were there with summer sleeping bags, summer clothes, summer boots, no gloves and no winter hats and we were freezing. And it wasn't until about two months later up around a place called Yong Dong Po that we got a shipment of winter sleeping bags believe me, that's the first time I got a good night sleep when I got my winter sleeping bag, the quilted bags and we got the heavier uniforms and boots and gloves. But Korea was... we weren't prepared for it.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How did your experiences in Korea differ from your World War II experience?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, you're being shot at so it's all the same thing. Either shoot them or they'll shoot you. It didn't. It was war. It was...

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Same thing, different place?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Different conditions and different terrain. How did the terrain differ in Korea than in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, it was mountains, cold mountains in Korea. I got to say one thing though. I was with the 3rd Division which was a good combat division. I got a message when I was up in the line to report back to company headquarters. I did. Company first sergeant, he said, you're to report to the battalion headquarter. I said, what for? He said, I don't know. I reported to battalion headquarter to a Major and he said, well you've got to report to regimental headquarters. He said he didn't know why. Regiment said, report to division headquarters.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Man, you must have been in big trouble.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I know. I know. I said, what did I do? What did I steal, you know? But I got down to division headquarters and division sergeant major had my records there and he says, I understand you were a reporter, a newspaper man. I said, yeah. He said what are you doing carrying a rifle? I said, they gave it to me and I had to go. He said the General wants to see you. I said, the General? I'm just a lowly sergeant. He said oh, no. We're going to talk to you. So they took me into an old school house that wasn't blown down and they put me in a room and behind a desk a guy with two big stars on his thing. It was General Souel, S-o-u-e-l, he says, "Young man, I understand you were a reporter." I said, "yes, sir." He said, "do you like this division?" I said, "yes, sir." He said, "do you got anything to say about this division?" "No, sir." Everything was "sir," you know. He said, do you know why you're here? I said, no, sir. I'd like to know, sir. He said, well, I'll tell you. We've got the Marines on our flank and all I see in the daily newspaper, the State Newspaper, the Marines did this. The Marines did that and we're doing more than they did. I want you to run a public information operation and report on what the 3rd Infantry Division done is doing and let's show the American public that the 3rd Infantry Division is doing it's part in Korea. In other words, he said, there's one thing about these damn Marines, he said they've got one of them fighting, another writing, and the other rotating. (Audio interruption with coughing.)

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: All right. You were telling me... so you were at division headquarters and they were going to have you write an article about

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Okay. Now, what I did, I got carte blanche from a Major General to do what I wanted to do as a staff sergeant. So he gave me a jeep, he gave me a driver, he gave me a tent, he gave me ability to go to Tokyo or have somebody to go to Tokyo to get primarily booze and liquor and bring it back and set up a press tent for the civilian press, associated press, Chicago Tribune, and New York Times, and whatever. So I set up a press tent and I also had good food shipped in. Canned food, caviar, and I passed the word around to the civilian correspondents over there that the 3rd Division Press Tent has got good booze, no cheap stuff, good food, no cheap stuff, plus we got cots with air mattresses on it and blankets and they started coming in. Then I would say, you want to go out on a mission? They say yeah. So we had at that time the 555th Heavy Tank Battalion and we had the new paten tanks with the 90 millimeter canon on it. And that was a five man crew. One of the front crewman was a machine gunner and we could take him out in the thing and put a civilian correspondent in there and he look through the scope and see what's happening over there. So I started saying we'll send you on a mission with the tanks. So they went in there. Of course, after they got shot at and got __ and everything else, they came back and they wrote a hell of a story on it. I got attacked. I'm on hill so and so. So we started getting good publicity on it because they'd say a tank from the 3rd Infantry Division. And then the General called me in or he didn't call me. He called me or he left a message for me. He says, I wanted to let you know that I'm very happy with the progress of your work and the ability to get my name and the division in the newspaper. I said Okay. He said keep it up so I did. Everything week they used to have a "fat cat flight." C 47 from Souel Airbase or __ Airbase Korea to Tokyo or Yokohama. And this is an airplane where the high high ranking people would put in fresh meat, fresh milk, fresh eggs, and I could take so many cubic feet for that aircraft was marked "Supplies: 3rd Infantry Division" and I had a representative over in Tokyo buy the liquor, buy the food. As a matter of fact they used to accuse me of running a booze and broads operation. The only thing I didn't supply was prostitutes but it worked. And it got to a point now... well, I got some extra help from the States. I got these young kids that went to journalism school, and they told me to train them. The Major says these are your people. So they did pretty well. They were young kids. Oh, at that time I was up in my 20s and they thought I was an old man. So I got more and more publicity with these young kids going out all gun hoe writing this and writing that and interviewing and everything else. And we got more and more space in the paper. And, of course, the General recognized that and I used to do a mass of press releases. We used to have our daily K.I.A., W.I.A., M.I.A. killed in action, wounded in action, missing in action. And I used to take the killed, those that we killed primarily Chinese at that time and we killed a thousand Chinese yesterday. We wounded 500 others and I put these press releases out. Well, the 3rd Infantry Division is doing knocking all these enemies down. One time this guy came up to me, he says, Bill, you know what you're doing? You're killing more of the enemy on paper than we're killing in the field. Which was true. Which was true. This was what the General wanted. We killed one, I said 10. We killed 10, I said 20. So but that was my job. That's what we wanted me to do and I was a good soldier. I obeyed orders. And I want to tell you one other thing. Just before I was going to leave when the war, the __ conference were being held, I was going to be sent back to the States, he gave me a Bronze Star for Meritorious Service.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: I guess he did appreciate what you did. How long did you do this new job?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, a year.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you like that better than being a rifleman?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you actually write any of the stories or did you just manage the whole tent?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I put the finishing touches on all the stories.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What was your title there? What did they call you?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: What did they call me? Sergeant.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Oh, when did you get made staff sergeant? Last I knew you were corporal.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: That's in World War II. When I got over into the 3rd Division.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: They immediately promoted you as staff sergeant?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What did being a staff sergeant get you that the corporal didn't?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What were the benefits of being a staff sergeant? You must have gotten more pay.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: More responsibility or did you do the same job?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, no matter what rank you had, if you were told to do a job, you did it. Primarily got more pay and theoretically you'd supervisor more men but in my case, no.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And actually once you went to do the newspaper, how many men did you have under you? Just the guys working on the reporting?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I had... maximum I had five. Well, I have four and one driver because the General gave me a jeep and a driver.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: That is pretty good. Were you living conditions better also?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: You bet. Being on the line? Of course.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Where did you stay when you were now?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I had my own tent.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Oh, your very own?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I had my own Korea man servant. Yeah. A Korea woman was washing my clothes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And was your food better too?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How did he find out that you were a newspaper man?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I guess he was getting fed up with not getting publicity. So he told somebody in the division headquarters go through the records of these Reservist coming over here. See if you can find any advertising man or newspaper man or public relations man so I can use them. So they went through the records and my name popped up and oh, yeah he went to Suffolk University and worked on this paper and that paper and that's how it happened.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And then you were sent back home. Do you remember when you got your recorders to go back to the United States?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. But I came back in December of '51.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And you went back into San Francisco?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Back... same train ride, Fort Devens, Massachusetts back into Boston.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And then were you discharged or were you still in the Reserves?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I was released to inactive service. See, when I was in the... I served three years in the Reserves, but before the three years was up, I was recalled to active duty and when I was in active duty the U.S. Congress extended my service for another three years. So, we didn't know it but that's what happened.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And how long were you on inactive service?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, until about 1953, I guess.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you have any duties or responsibilities?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And then you were officially discharged in 1953.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I was released from Reserve status to civilian status.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What did you do when you came back from Korea and you were on inactive service? Did you go back to the paper in Cape Cod?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I went... I was still wearing my uniform there because I was 6'3 and I took a 39 XL and they didn't have it. So I got my father's car and I went down looking for jobs and bigger newspapers. And I started the Bridge Board Post and then I went to New Haven register and the __ Journal, the record journal. That was about 3 o'clock in the afternoon I met Carter White, the publisher. He says, Okay, fill out the application. I'll see what I can do. And then at 5 o'clock I stopped in Hartford and the last place on my list was the Hartford Times. It was supposed to be the biggest, and it was at that time. So I went into the building. The city editor was gone, the manager was gone, they were all gone. So I went to see some assistant. He said, well, they won't be back until tomorrow. I said, well who's doing the hiring and firing? He said, well, nobody. So I walked down the hall and saw a sign that says "publisher's officer, do not enter." So I said, well, the hell with it. So I walked in. I saw a sign that said, "Private, do not enter." So I opened the door and walked in. This man looked up and said, "who are you?" I said, I'm Bill Huebner from Boston. I'm a newspaper man. I'm coming back from Korea. I still have my uniform on. I'm looking for a job. He said, oh, is that right? He said, sit down, young man, and we'll talk about it. He interviewed me verbally. Nothing in writing and he says give me your telephone number where you can be reached in Watertown, Mas. So he says, I'll let you know. So Monday morning my mother says you got a call from somebody in Hartford. I said, Okay. Who is it? It's Mr. Murphy, Francis S. Murphy, who was publisher of the Hartford Times. He says, young man, can you get down here? He called everybody "young man." He says, young man, can you get down here this afternoon? I want to talk to you. I said, yes, sir. So I borrowed a set of clothes. They didn't fit me very well and I drove down to Hartford. I went to Mr. Murphy's office and he says, sit down, young man. I said, yes, sir. And he says, you know what I'm going to do? I'm going to hire you. I said, well, thank you, sir. He said, I don't even know your credentials. He said, but I'm hiring you for this reason: I've got a secretary here, an assistant secretary, I've got assistant to the publisher to keep people like you out of my office. He says, but that's what I want in a newspaper man. Somebody that doesn't obey these signs and goes around and gets the story and you did just that and you came right to me. Asked for a job flat out. He says, that's what I want in a newspaper man. You're hired. Report to so and so. And so that's why I spent 25 years at the Hartford Times.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Wow. What were you duties there?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, I was a reporter. I covered a lot of things. I covered police, I covered the legislature, general assignment. I was at one time a senior state reporter covering the bureaus around the state. And I ended up as the real estate and development editor for the Sunday Times and then I knew the paper was going down the tubes so I had my retirement in. So I quit. In the mean time, I was hired by the Connecticut Roadbuilders Association as director of public affairs and I stayed there 18 years.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Now, when you got your job at Hartford Times, you must have moved to Connecticut at that point?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And is that when you moved to Avon?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. I moved to Windsor Locks and I lived in Windsor Locks and Mr. Murphy was ...although he was the publisher of the Hartford Times, he was also the chairman of the State Aeronautics Commission. And one of his babies was development of Bradley Airport at that time. And he says I want you to live in Windsor Locks and I want you to cover that airport. Everything about the airport because eventually it's going to be a big international airport. That's a long time ago. That man had a foresight. So I moved to Windsor Locks in a furnished room and eventually bought a house in Windsor Locks, and I covered the airport, and I covered aviation. I eventually became an aviation writer for the Times but he was a good man. Francis S. Murphy was a good man.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Wow. Did you stay in touch with any of your fellow soldiers or officers from Korea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes. One was Major John Danzinbaker who was a battalion executive who theoretically was my supervisor, but he didn't do much supervising because everything was going so fine. He was getting credit too. So we became good friends and he lived up in Marlboro, Massachusetts. He's dead now. He was a good man. Oh, I forget his name now. He was...he ended up as the editor of the Green Wood Mississippi Times a newspaper down there. Oh, another one was Oakland California Tribune. So we're all spread around.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did you join any veteran's organizations?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I belong to VFW.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And what's the post number?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: 3272 Avon.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And when did you join the VFW?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Actually, I joined them in... Oh, 15 years ago.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: What are the activities that your VFW post engages in?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, well they have The Voice of Democracy Contest for school children. They field speakers on World War II and Korea and Vietnam, to the high schools and the junior high schools. And I was part of that telling the youngsters what the military is all about. And other sundry things is all. We, anybody dies, we have a funeral for them, fire a rifle. Eileen Hurst:: And you retired from the Connecticut Roadbuilders Association?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: And you've been retired since and living in Avon?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or the military in general?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I smartened up. That's all. We need a good strong military because we were caught off guard with Pearl Harbor without a strong military and we were even caught off guard in Korea without a strong military. So I've always been a strong supporter of military appropriation, and that's one reason why I worked on Ronald Reagan's campaign, two campaigns because of his budgets to improve the military. Get new equipment, new aircraft, et cetera, et cetera. I worked on two of his campaigns raising funds.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you attend any reunions?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Of what?

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Military reunions. Either for World War II or Korea.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: I belong to the society for the 3rd Infantry Division. I haven't attended any reunions.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: How did your service and experiences affect your life?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Well, it's the old story: You went into the army as a boy and came out a man. That's about the size of it.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: So you agree with that?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Do you think you helped the young men who were inexperienced in Korea because of your experience?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: That's true. What you said is true, but you've got to remember, I was there to save my own fanny and in doing so, I saved theirs. To smarten them up and because I had to be smartened up by some of my platoon sergeants in World War II.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Have you been down to Washington, D.C. to see the Korea memorial?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Is there anything else that you'd like to add that we haven't covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No. I guess you've done pretty well.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Any other stories or incidents that you can remember either about World War II or Korea?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: There's a lot but I don't want to go on record with it.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Okay. Anything else that you'd like to add?

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: No, not at this time.

sp.speaker: Eileen Hurst
sp.p: Well, I'd like to thank you, Bill, for supporting this project and thank you for your time and thank you for your service.

sp.speaker: William Huebner
sp.p: Okay.
